claim: CRM1 is a highly conserved, RanGTPase-driven exportin that carries proteins and RNPs from the nucleus to the cytoplasm.
source: CRM1 is a highly conserved, RanGTPase-driven exportin that carries proteins and RNPs from the nucleus to the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CRM1 function, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: More than 700 export substrates were identified from the yeast S. cerevisiae.
source: We now explored the cargo-spectrum of CRM1 in depth and identified surprisingly large numbers, namely >700 export substrates from the yeast S. cerevisiae, ≈1000 from Xenopus oocytes and >1050 from human cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data presented in the study.

claim: Approximately 1000 export substrates were identified from Xenopus oocytes.
source: We now explored the cargo-spectrum of CRM1 in depth and identified surprisingly large numbers, namely >700 export substrates from the yeast S. cerevisiae, ≈1000 from Xenopus oocytes and >1050 from human cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data presented in the study.

claim: More than 1050 export substrates were identified from human cells.
source: We now explored the cargo-spectrum of CRM1 in depth and identified surprisingly large numbers, namely >700 export substrates from the yeast S. cerevisiae, ≈1000 from Xenopus oocytes and >1050 from human cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data presented in the study.

claim: The partitioning of approximately 5000 unique proteins between nucleus and cytoplasm of Xenopus oocytes was quantified.
source: In addition, we quantified the partitioning of ≈5000 unique proteins between nucleus and cytoplasm of Xenopus oocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: CRM1 has new functions in spatial control of vesicle coat-assembly.
source: The data suggest new CRM1 functions in spatial control of vesicle coat-assembly, centrosomes, autophagy, peroxisome biogenesis, cytoskeleton, ribosome maturation, translation, mRNA degradation, and more generally in precluding a potentially detrimental action of cytoplasmic pathways within the nuclear interior.
evidence: This is inferred from the identification of vesicle coat proteins as CRM1 cargoes in the study.

claim: CRM1 has new functions in spatial control of centrosomes.
source: The data suggest new CRM1 functions in spatial control of vesicle coat-assembly, centrosomes, autophagy, peroxisome biogenesis, cytoskeleton, ribosome maturation, translation, mRNA degradation, and more generally in precluding a potentially detrimental action of cytoplasmic pathways within the nuclear interior.
evidence: This is inferred from the identification of centrosomal proteins as CRM1 cargoes in the study.

claim: CRM1 has new functions in spatial control of autophagy.
source: The data suggest new CRM1 functions in spatial control of vesicle coat-assembly, centrosomes, autophagy, peroxisome biogenesis, cytoskeleton, ribosome maturation, translation, mRNA degradation, and more generally in precluding a potentially detrimental action of cytoplasmic pathways within the nuclear interior.
evidence: This is inferred from the identification of autophagy-related proteins as CRM1 cargoes in the study.

claim: CRM1 has new functions in spatial control of peroxisome biogenesis.
source: The data suggest new CRM1 functions in spatial control of vesicle coat-assembly, centrosomes, autophagy, peroxisome biogenesis, cytoskeleton, ribosome maturation, translation, mRNA degradation, and more generally in precluding a potentially detrimental action of cytoplasmic pathways within the nuclear interior.
evidence: This is inferred from the identification of peroxisome biogenesis factors as CRM1 cargoes in the study.

evidence: This is inferred from the identification of ribosome maturation factors as CRM1 cargoes in the study.

claim: CRM1 has new functions in spatial control of translation.
source: The data suggest new CRM1 functions in spatial control of vesicle coat-assembly, centrosomes, autophagy, peroxisome biogenesis, cytoskeleton, ribosome maturation, translation, mRNA degradation, and more generally in precluding a potentially detrimental action of cytoplasmic pathways within the nuclear interior.

claim: CRM1 has new functions in spatial control of mRNA degradation.

claim: CRM1 precludes a potentially detrimental action of cytoplasmic pathways within the nuclear interior.
source: The data suggest new CRM1 functions in spatial control of vesicle coat-assembly, centrosomes, autophagy, peroxisome biogenesis, cytoskeleton, ribosome maturation, translation, mRNA degradation, and more generally in precluding a potentially detrimental action of cytoplasmic pathways within the nuclear interior.
evidence: This is a general interpretation of the data showing CRM1-mediated export of cytoplasmic proteins from the nucleus.

claim: The NPC permeability barrier grants small molecules a free passage.
source: It grants small molecules a free passage, but becomes increasingly restrictive as the size of the mobile species approaches or exceeds a diameter of ≈ 5 nm (Mohr et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mohr et al., 2009.

claim: The NPC permeability barrier becomes increasingly restrictive as the size of the mobile species approaches or exceeds a diameter of approximately 5 nm.
source: It grants small molecules a free passage, but becomes increasingly restrictive as the size of the mobile species approaches or exceeds a diameter of ≈ 5 nm (Mohr et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mohr et al., 2009.

claim: Shuttling nuclear transport receptors can traverse NPCs by facilitated translocation.
source: Shuttling nuclear transport receptors (NTRs) are not bound by this restriction (for review see: Kimura and Imamoto, 2014). They can traverse NPCs by facilitated translocation and have the capacity to ferry even large cargoes, such as newly assembled ribosomal subunits, across the barrier.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Kimura and Imamoto, 2014.

claim: Nuclear transport receptors have the capacity to ferry even large cargoes, such as newly assembled ribosomal subunits, across the barrier.
source: They can traverse NPCs by facilitated translocation and have the capacity to ferry even large cargoes, such as newly assembled ribosomal subunits, across the barrier.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Kimura and Imamoto, 2014.

claim: Active transport of cargoes against concentration gradients requires an intact NE and NPC-barrier for retaining already transported cargoes in the destination compartment.
source: Active transport of cargoes against concentration gradients requires an intact NE and NPC-barrier for retaining already transported cargoes in the destination compartment.
evidence: This is established knowledge about nuclear transport mechanisms.

claim: Active transport requires an input of metabolic energy, typically by the RanGTPase system.
source: In addition, it requires an input of metabolic energy, typically by the RanGTPase system.
evidence: This is established knowledge about nuclear transport mechanisms.

claim: Exportins bind their cargo molecules cooperatively with RanGTP inside nuclei.
source: Exportins (reviewed in Güttler and Görlich, 2011) bind their cargo molecules cooperatively with RanGTP inside nuclei, carry them as trimeric RanGTP·exportin·cargo complexes to the cytoplasm, where GTP-hydrolysis triggers release of cargo and Ran.
evidence: This is established knowledge about exportin function, supported by citation to Güttler and Görlich, 2011.

claim: Exportins carry cargo as trimeric RanGTP·exportin·cargo complexes to the cytoplasm.
source: Exportins (reviewed in Güttler and Görlich, 2011) bind their cargo molecules cooperatively with RanGTP inside nuclei, carry them as trimeric RanGTP·exportin·cargo complexes to the cytoplasm, where GTP-hydrolysis triggers release of cargo and Ran.
evidence: This is established knowledge about exportin function, supported by citation to Güttler and Görlich, 2011.

claim: GTP-hydrolysis triggers release of cargo and Ran from exportins in the cytoplasm.
source: Exportins (reviewed in Güttler and Görlich, 2011) bind their cargo molecules cooperatively with RanGTP inside nuclei, carry them as trimeric RanGTP·exportin·cargo complexes to the cytoplasm, where GTP-hydrolysis triggers release of cargo and Ran.
evidence: This is established knowledge about exportin function, supported by citation to Güttler and Görlich, 2011.

claim: CRM1 is the most conserved nuclear export receptor.
source: CRM1, also called exportin 1 or Xpo1, is the most conserved nuclear export receptor (Adachi and Yanagida, 1989; Fornerod et al., 1997a; Fukuda et al., 1997; Stade et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to early CRM1 studies.

claim: CRM1 recognises its cargoes through short linear nuclear export signals (NESs).
source: CRM1 recognises its cargoes through short linear nuclear export signals (NESs), which comprise 4–5 critical hydrophobic (Φ) residues with characteristic spacings (Wen et al., 1994; Fischer et al., 1995; Dong et al., 2009; Monecke et al., 2009; Güttler et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: NESs comprise 4–5 critical hydrophobic residues with characteristic spacings.
source: CRM1 recognises its cargoes through short linear nuclear export signals (NESs), which comprise 4–5 critical hydrophobic (Φ) residues with characteristic spacings (Wen et al., 1994; Fischer et al., 1995; Dong et al., 2009; Monecke et al., 2009; Güttler et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: CRM1 is essential for viability.
source: CRM1 is essential for viability and is the target of the potentially lethal bacterial toxin leptomycin B (Nishi et al., 1994), which blocks NES-binding by covalently modifying a conserved cysteine residue within the NES-binding site (Kudo et al., 1999; Dong et al., 2009; Monecke et al., 2009; Sun et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nishi et al., 1994.

claim: Leptomycin B blocks NES-binding by covalently modifying a conserved cysteine residue within the NES-binding site.
source: CRM1 is essential for viability and is the target of the potentially lethal bacterial toxin leptomycin B (Nishi et al., 1994), which blocks NES-binding by covalently modifying a conserved cysteine residue within the NES-binding site (Kudo et al., 1999; Dong et al., 2009; Monecke et al., 2009; Sun et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: CRM1 carries newly assembled 40S and 60S ribosomal subunits.
source: CRM1 is known to carry multiple cargoes, including newly assembled 40S and 60S ribosomal subunits, the signal recognition particle SRP, U snRNAs, or the genomic RNA of HIV1 via the Rev protein (Moy and Silver, 1999; Ciufo and Brown, 2000; Ho et al., 2000; Ohno et al., 2000; Gadal et al., 2001; Thomas and Kutay, 2003; Rouquette et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: CRM1 carries the signal recognition particle SRP.
source: CRM1 is known to carry multiple cargoes, including newly assembled 40S and 60S ribosomal subunits, the signal recognition particle SRP, U snRNAs, or the genomic RNA of HIV1 via the Rev protein (Moy and Silver, 1999; Ciufo and Brown, 2000; Ho et al., 2000; Ohno et al., 2000; Gadal et al., 2001; Thomas and Kutay, 2003; Rouquette et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: CRM1 carries U snRNAs.
source: CRM1 is known to carry multiple cargoes, including newly assembled 40S and 60S ribosomal subunits, the signal recognition particle SRP, U snRNAs, or the genomic RNA of HIV1 via the Rev protein (Moy and Silver, 1999; Ciufo and Brown, 2000; Ho et al., 2000; Ohno et al., 2000; Gadal et al., 2001; Thomas and Kutay, 2003; Rouquette et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: CRM1 carries the genomic RNA of HIV1 via the Rev protein.
source: CRM1 is known to carry multiple cargoes, including newly assembled 40S and 60S ribosomal subunits, the signal recognition particle SRP, U snRNAs, or the genomic RNA of HIV1 via the Rev protein (Moy and Silver, 1999; Ciufo and Brown, 2000; Ho et al., 2000; Ohno et al., 2000; Gadal et al., 2001; Thomas and Kutay, 2003; Rouquette et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Intranuclear protein synthesis would be a wasteful process because ribosomes would translate unspliced or incompletely spliced mRNAs.
source: Intranuclear protein synthesis, for example, would be a particularly wasteful process, because ribosomes would then also translate unspliced or incompletely spliced mRNAs, consequently read into introns, add inappropriate residues to the nascent chains, eventually encounter premature stop codons and thus produce truncated protein fragments.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on known biology of mRNA splicing and translation.

claim: Aberrant translation products from intranuclear translation would be non-functional and probably toxic.
source: Such aberrant translation products would not only be non-functional, but probably also toxic, because they fail to fold, or act in a dominant-negative fashion.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on protein folding principles.

claim: The NE acts as a primary barrier to keep cytoplasmic translation activity out of nuclei.
source: It is thus not very surprising that eukaryotic cells have implemented several lines of defence against intranuclear translation, whereby the NE acts as a primary barrier to keep cytoplasmic translation activity out of nuclei.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the compartmentalization of translation.

claim: 40S and 60S ribosomal subunits gain full translation competence only following late maturation steps in the cytoplasm.
source: Likewise, even though the 40S and 60S ribosomal subunits assemble inside the nucleus, they gain full translation competence only following late maturation steps in the cytoplasm (reviewed in Panse and Johnson, 2010; Thomson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to reviews on ribosome maturation.

claim: Objects larger than the nominal exclusion limit can leak into the nucleus.
source: A very general problem is, however, that the NPC barrier is not perfect. Instead, also objects larger than the nominal exclusion limit can leak—albeit slowly—into the nucleus (Bonner, 1975; Mohr et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bonner, 1975 and Mohr et al., 2009.

claim: Animal Xpo6 keeps actin out of the nucleus.
source: Animal Xpo6, for example, keeps actin out of the nucleus (Stüven et al., 2003), while Xpo4 and Xpo5 do the same for the translation elongation factors eIF5a (Lipowsky et al., 2000) and eEF1A respectively (Bohnsack et al., 2002; Calado et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stüven et al., 2003.

claim: Xpo4 keeps the translation elongation factor eIF5a out of the nucleus.
source: Animal Xpo6, for example, keeps actin out of the nucleus (Stüven et al., 2003), while Xpo4 and Xpo5 do the same for the translation elongation factors eIF5a (Lipowsky et al., 2000) and eEF1A respectively (Bohnsack et al., 2002; Calado et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lipowsky et al., 2000.

claim: Xpo5 keeps the translation elongation factor eEF1A out of the nucleus.
source: Animal Xpo6, for example, keeps actin out of the nucleus (Stüven et al., 2003), while Xpo4 and Xpo5 do the same for the translation elongation factors eIF5a (Lipowsky et al., 2000) and eEF1A respectively (Bohnsack et al., 2002; Calado et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bohnsack et al., 2002 and Calado et al., 2002.

claim: CRM1 expels RanBP1 from the nuclear compartment.
source: CRM1 was shown to expel several cytoplasmic factors from the nuclear compartment, including the RanGTPase system components RanBP1 (Plafker and Macara, 2000) and RanGAP (Feng et al., 1999) as well as the translation factor subunits eIF2β, eIF5, eIF2Bε and eRF1 (Bohnsack et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Plafker and Macara, 2000.

claim: CRM1 expels RanGAP from the nuclear compartment.
source: CRM1 was shown to expel several cytoplasmic factors from the nuclear compartment, including the RanGTPase system components RanBP1 (Plafker and Macara, 2000) and RanGAP (Feng et al., 1999) as well as the translation factor subunits eIF2β, eIF5, eIF2Bε and eRF1 (Bohnsack et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Feng et al., 1999.

claim: CRM1 expels the translation factor subunits eIF2β, eIF5, eIF2Bε and eRF1 from the nuclear compartment.
source: CRM1 was shown to expel several cytoplasmic factors from the nuclear compartment, including the RanGTPase system components RanBP1 (Plafker and Macara, 2000) and RanGAP (Feng et al., 1999) as well as the translation factor subunits eIF2β, eIF5, eIF2Bε and eRF1 (Bohnsack et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bohnsack et al., 2002.

claim: Xenopus laevis stage VI oocytes measure approximately 1.3 mm in diameter.
source: In order to avoid these problems, we turned to Xenopus laevis stage VI oocytes (Dumont, 1972). These cells measure ≈1.3 mm in diameter and have nuclei of ≈450 µm.
evidence: This is a measurement of oocyte size, supported by citation to Dumont, 1972.

claim: Xenopus laevis stage VI oocyte nuclei measure approximately 450 µm.
source: In order to avoid these problems, we turned to Xenopus laevis stage VI oocytes (Dumont, 1972). These cells measure ≈1.3 mm in diameter and have nuclei of ≈450 µm.
evidence: This is a measurement of nuclear size, supported by citation to Dumont, 1972.

claim: The large dimensions of Xenopus oocytes allow for manual dissection into nuclear and cytoplasmic fractions with exceptionally little cross-contamination.
source: Such very large dimensions allow for a manual oocyte dissection into nuclear and cytoplasmic fractions with exceptionally little cross-contamination (see e.g. De Robertis et al., 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citation to De Robertis et al., 1978.

claim: The volume of Xenopus oocyte nuclei is 100,000 times larger than that of average-sized cells with a G2 DNA content.
source: These oocyte nuclei are also special with their volume being 100,000 times larger than that of average-sized cells with a G2 DNA contents.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the measured nuclear size.

claim: A total of 9573 proteoforms were identified in the Xenopus oocyte nucleocytoplasmic partitioning analysis.
source: In this way, a total of 9573 proteoforms (Smith et al., 2013) were identified, 7015 in isolated nuclei and 7036 in the cytoplasmic fractions.
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of the mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: 7015 proteoforms were identified in isolated nuclei of Xenopus oocytes.
source: In this way, a total of 9573 proteoforms (Smith et al., 2013) were identified, 7015 in isolated nuclei and 7036 in the cytoplasmic fractions.
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of the mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: 7036 proteoforms were identified in the cytoplasmic fractions of Xenopus oocytes.
source: In this way, a total of 9573 proteoforms (Smith et al., 2013) were identified, 7015 in isolated nuclei and 7036 in the cytoplasmic fractions.
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of the mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: 4478 proteoforms were identified in both nuclear and cytoplasmic fractions of Xenopus oocytes.
source: The intersection set comprised 4478 proteoforms (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and stated in the text.

claim: A total of 5006 unique proteins were identified after filtering for contaminants in Xenopus oocytes.
source: This left us with a total of 5006 unique proteins. Of these, 1126 were identified only in the nuclear fraction, 1059 only in cytosolic fraction and 2821 in both compartments (Figure 1D, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D and stated in the text.

claim: 1126 unique proteins were identified only in the nuclear fraction of Xenopus oocytes.
source: This left us with a total of 5006 unique proteins. Of these, 1126 were identified only in the nuclear fraction, 1059 only in cytosolic fraction and 2821 in both compartments (Figure 1D, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D and stated in the text.

claim: 1059 unique proteins were identified only in the cytosolic fraction of Xenopus oocytes.
source: This left us with a total of 5006 unique proteins. Of these, 1126 were identified only in the nuclear fraction, 1059 only in cytosolic fraction and 2821 in both compartments (Figure 1D, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D and stated in the text.

claim: 2821 unique proteins were identified in both nuclear and cytoplasmic compartments of Xenopus oocytes.
source: This left us with a total of 5006 unique proteins. Of these, 1126 were identified only in the nuclear fraction, 1059 only in cytosolic fraction and 2821 in both compartments (Figure 1D, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D and stated in the text.

claim: Nucleophosmin has a nuclear concentration of approximately 2.3 µM in Xenopus oocytes.
source: For nucleophosmin (a histone chaperone), we measured a nuclear concentration of ≈ 2.3 µM, a cytoplasmic concentration of 8 nM, and hence a nucleocytoplasmic (N:C) partition coefficient of 300:1.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the mass spectrometry data.

claim: Nucleophosmin has a cytoplasmic concentration of 8 nM in Xenopus oocytes.
source: For nucleophosmin (a histone chaperone), we measured a nuclear concentration of ≈ 2.3 µM, a cytoplasmic concentration of 8 nM, and hence a nucleocytoplasmic (N:C) partition coefficient of 300:1.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the mass spectrometry data.

claim: Nucleophosmin has a nucleocytoplasmic partition coefficient of 300:1 in Xenopus oocytes.
source: For nucleophosmin (a histone chaperone), we measured a nuclear concentration of ≈ 2.3 µM, a cytoplasmic concentration of 8 nM, and hence a nucleocytoplasmic (N:C) partition coefficient of 300:1.
evidence: This is calculated from the measured concentrations.

claim: Gelsolin has a nuclear concentration of approximately 0.01 µM in Xenopus oocytes.
source: For gelsolin (a factor that stabilizes cytoplasmic actin in its G-form) we measured a nuclear concentration of ≈ 0.01 µM, a cytoplasmic of ≈ 4 µM, and thus an N:C ratio of 1:400.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the mass spectrometry data.

claim: Gelsolin has a cytoplasmic concentration of approximately 4 µM in Xenopus oocytes.
source: For gelsolin (a factor that stabilizes cytoplasmic actin in its G-form) we measured a nuclear concentration of ≈ 0.01 µM, a cytoplasmic of ≈ 4 µM, and thus an N:C ratio of 1:400.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the mass spectrometry data.

claim: Gelsolin has a nucleocytoplasmic ratio of 1:400 in Xenopus oocytes.
source: For gelsolin (a factor that stabilizes cytoplasmic actin in its G-form) we measured a nuclear concentration of ≈ 0.01 µM, a cytoplasmic of ≈ 4 µM, and thus an N:C ratio of 1:400.
evidence: This is calculated from the measured concentrations.

claim: The obtained nuclear and cytoplasmic fractions show only very limited cross-contamination.
source: This suggests that the obtained nuclear and cytoplasmic fractions show only very limited cross-contamination and also suggested what range of partition coefficients should be expected also for other proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the extreme partition coefficients of marker proteins.

claim: Oocyte nuclei contain all glycolytic enzymes, except for hexokinase and phosphofructokinase.
source: The oocyte nucleus contains all glycolytic enzymes, except for hexokinase and phosphofructokinase that catalyse the ATP-consuming preparatory steps.
evidence: This is based on the mass spectrometry data showing the presence or absence of these enzymes.

claim: 6-phosphofructokinase (PFK) is confined to the cytoplasm with an N:C ratio of approximately 1:2000.
source: The hexokinase level is generally very low in oocytes (because they produce glucose 6-phosphate by other means; see Nutt et al., 2005 and Supplementary file 1), while 6-phosphofructokinase (PFK) is confined to the cytoplasm (N:C ≈ 1:2000; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the mass spectrometry data.

claim: The enzyme distribution predicts a directed flux of fructose 1,6 bisphosphate into the nucleus.
source: This enzyme distribution predicts a directed flux of fructose 1,6 bisphosphate into the nucleus.
evidence: This is inferred from the distribution of glycolytic enzymes.

claim: Oocyte nuclei produce the high-energy compounds phosphoenolpyruvate and 1,3 bisphoglycerate locally.
source: It further suggests that oocyte nuclei produce the high-energy compounds phosphoenolpyruvate and 1,3 bisphoglycerate locally and use them for synthesizing ATP and other NTPs.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of glycolytic enzymes in the nucleus.

claim: Oocytes enable a creatine phosphate energy shuttle by maintaining high creatine kinase concentrations in both cytoplasm and nucleus (3 µM and 1.5 µM, respectively).
source: Oocytes enable such CP shuttle by maintaining high CK concentrations in both, cytoplasm and nucleus (3 µM and 1.5 µM, respectively; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on the measured concentrations of creatine kinase.

claim: Approximately 2800 proteins were identified in Xenopus starting extracts for CRM1 affinity chromatography.
source: Using the mass-spectrometric approaches mentioned above, we identified in the starting extracts ≈2800 (Xenopus), ≈3900 (human) and ≈2600 (yeast) proteins (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and stated in the text.

claim: Approximately 3900 proteins were identified in human starting extracts for CRM1 affinity chromatography.
source: Using the mass-spectrometric approaches mentioned above, we identified in the starting extracts ≈2800 (Xenopus), ≈3900 (human) and ≈2600 (yeast) proteins (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and stated in the text.

claim: Approximately 2600 proteins were identified in yeast starting extracts for CRM1 affinity chromatography.
source: Using the mass-spectrometric approaches mentioned above, we identified in the starting extracts ≈2800 (Xenopus), ≈3900 (human) and ≈2600 (yeast) proteins (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and stated in the text.

claim: Approximately 2300 proteins were identified in the Xenopus 'CRM1+RanGTP' samples.
source: In the 'CRM1+RanGTP' samples, ≈2300, 3000 and ≈2000 proteins were identified.
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of the mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: Approximately 3000 proteins were identified in the human 'CRM1+RanGTP' samples.
source: In the 'CRM1+RanGTP' samples, ≈2300, 3000 and ≈2000 proteins were identified.
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of the mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: Approximately 2000 proteins were identified in the yeast 'CRM1+RanGTP' samples.
source: In the 'CRM1+RanGTP' samples, ≈2300, 3000 and ≈2000 proteins were identified.
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of the mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: About 14% of proteins identified in 'CRM1+RanGTP' samples had not been detected in the total extracts.
source: About 14% of these had not been detected in the total extracts and these probably represent low-abundance proteins that had been highly enriched during CRM1 affinity chromatography.
evidence: This is calculated from the mass spectrometry data.

claim: The majority of identified CRM1 cargoes are proteins and protein complexes with a very strong bias towards a cytoplasmic localisation.
source: The majority of identified CRM1 cargoes are proteins and protein complexes with a very strong bias towards a cytoplasmic localisation, suggesting that their active back-sorting from the nucleus is a major cellular activity.
evidence: This is based on the nucleocytoplasmic partitioning data and CRM1 binding data.

claim: Active back-sorting of cytoplasmic proteins from the nucleus is a major cellular activity.
source: The majority of identified CRM1 cargoes are proteins and protein complexes with a very strong bias towards a cytoplasmic localisation, suggesting that their active back-sorting from the nucleus is a major cellular activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the large number of cytoplasmic CRM1 cargoes.

claim: Nearly all translation factors are CRM1 cargoes.
source: This applies to nearly all translation factors (including the largest translation factor complexes like eIF2B), to factors involved in final ribosomal maturation steps, which might prevent ribosomes from acquiring translation competence already in the nuclear compartment, as well as to regulatory proteins, autophagy-linked factors, peroxisome biogenesis factors and to centrosomal proteins, in both, humans and frogs.
evidence: This is based on the CRM1 binding data for translation factors.

claim: Factors involved in final ribosomal maturation steps are CRM1 cargoes.
source: This applies to nearly all translation factors (including the largest translation factor complexes like eIF2B), to factors involved in final ribosomal maturation steps, which might prevent ribosomes from acquiring translation competence already in the nuclear compartment, as well as to regulatory proteins, autophagy-linked factors, peroxisome biogenesis factors and to centrosomal proteins, in both, humans and frogs.
evidence: This is based on the CRM1 binding data for ribosomal maturation factors.

claim: CRM1-mediated export of ribosomal maturation factors might prevent ribosomes from acquiring translation competence already in the nuclear compartment.
source: This applies to nearly all translation factors (including the largest translation factor complexes like eIF2B), to factors involved in final ribosomal maturation steps, which might prevent ribosomes from acquiring translation competence already in the nuclear compartment, as well as to regulatory proteins, autophagy-linked factors, peroxisome biogenesis factors and to centrosomal proteins, in both, humans and frogs.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Vesicle coat proteins are CRM1 cargoes with perfect nuclear exclusion.
source: Another major functional group of CRM1 cargoes with perfect nuclear exclusion is represented by vesicle coat proteins, which points to a strong evolutionary pressure to preclude the budding of vesicles from the inner nuclear membrane.
evidence: This is based on the CRM1 binding data and nucleocytoplasmic partitioning data for vesicle coat proteins.

claim: There is strong evolutionary pressure to preclude the budding of vesicles from the inner nuclear membrane.
source: Another major functional group of CRM1 cargoes with perfect nuclear exclusion is represented by vesicle coat proteins, which points to a strong evolutionary pressure to preclude the budding of vesicles from the inner nuclear membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the perfect nuclear exclusion of vesicle coat proteins.

claim: 23 out of 29 tested candidates were validated as CRM1 cargoes.
source: In total, we tested 29 candidates from Xenopus, human and yeast, and validated 23 of them positive (Figures 4, 6, 7 and 8), suggesting that the majority of hits represent indeed CRM1 cargoes.
evidence: This is based on the transfection assays shown in the figures.

claim: The majority of hits represent CRM1 cargoes.
source: In total, we tested 29 candidates from Xenopus, human and yeast, and validated 23 of them positive (Figures 4, 6, 7 and 8), suggesting that the majority of hits represent indeed CRM1 cargoes.
evidence: This is inferred from the high validation rate.

claim: eRF3a is a CRM1 cargo with an NES within the N-terminal unstructured region.
source: We identified this NES within the N-terminal unstructured region of eRF3a and confirmed its nuclear export activity by transfection assays as well (Figure 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 with transfection assays.

claim: eRF3a binds purified CRM1 in a RanGTP-dependent manner.
source: eRF3a binds also purified CRM1 in a RanGTP-dependent manner (Figure 5), suggesting that the interaction is direct and not bridged by another factor.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5 with binding assays.

claim: The 1b subunit of the Arp2/3 complex is a directly-binding, bona fide CRM1 export cargo with an NES at its extreme C-terminus.
source: Next, we also confirmed a far lower scoring 'category B' candidate, namely the 1b subunit of the Arp2/3 complex, as a directly-binding, bona fide CRM1 export cargo with an NES at its extreme C-terminus.
evidence: This is based on transfection assays and binding assays shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Many highly abundant metabolic enzymes show a rather even distribution between cytoplasm and nucleus of the Xenopus oocyte without having a detectable NLS.
source: Here, it is remarkable that many of these CRM1 non-cargoes, including enzymes that are part of large complexes, show a rather even distribution between cytoplasm and nucleus of the Xenopus oocyte without having a detectable NLS (Supplementary file 2, sheets 'glycolysis' and 'metabolic enzymes').
evidence: This is based on the nucleocytoplasmic partitioning data.

claim: A large size alone cannot guarantee a cytoplasmic confinement.
source: This suggests that a large size alone cannot guarantee a cytoplasmic confinement.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that large complexes can equilibrate between nucleus and cytoplasm.

claim: eIF2, eIF2B, eIF4B, eIF4G, eIF5 and eIF5B all behaved like high-scoring cargoes in either Xenopus, human or yeast.
source: eIF2, eIF2B, eIF4B, eIF4G, eIF5 and eIF5B all behaved like high-scoring cargoes in either Xenopus, human or yeast, which coincides nicely with their complete exclusion from the nuclei of Xenopus oocytes.
evidence: This is based on the CRM1 binding data and nucleocytoplasmic partitioning data.

claim: Translation initiation factors show complete exclusion from the nuclei of Xenopus oocytes.
source: eIF2, eIF2B, eIF4B, eIF4G, eIF5 and eIF5B all behaved like high-scoring cargoes in either Xenopus, human or yeast, which coincides nicely with their complete exclusion from the nuclei of Xenopus oocytes.
evidence: This is based on the nucleocytoplasmic partitioning data.

claim: CRM1 serves the purpose of suppressing intranuclear translation by exporting translation factors.
source: We assume that CRM1 serves here the purpose of suppressing intranuclear translation and possibly also avoiding an interference with ribosome biogenesis if translation factors bound pre-maturely to ribosomal assembly intermediates.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Even very large translation factor complexes behaved like nuclear export substrates.
source: It is therefore remarkable that even very large translation factor complexes behaved like nuclear export substrates, examples being the 125 kDa eIF2αβγ complex (150 kDa with tRNA) or the 270 kDa eIF2Bαβγδε complex (Supplementary files 2–4, sheets 'Translation factors').
evidence: This is based on the CRM1 binding data for these complexes.

claim: Even the presumably slow leakage of large cytoplasmic assemblies into nuclei can be so deleterious that countermeasures are required.
source: This suggests that even the presumably slow leakage of large cytoplasmic assemblies into nuclei can be so deleterious that countermeasures are required.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that large translation factor complexes are CRM1 cargoes.

claim: Human EF1A was previously identified as the most prominent export cargo of Xpo5.
source: Human EF1A was previously identified as the most prominent export cargo of Xpo5, while the elongation factor for proline-rich regions, eIF5A, is exported by Xpo4 (Lipowsky et al., 2000; Bohnsack et al., 2002; Calado et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: eIF5A is exported by Xpo4.
source: Human EF1A was previously identified as the most prominent export cargo of Xpo5, while the elongation factor for proline-rich regions, eIF5A, is exported by Xpo4 (Lipowsky et al., 2000; Bohnsack et al., 2002; Calado et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The translation termination factor eRF3a is a bona fide CRM1 cargo.
source: The translation termination factor eRF3a is again a bona fide CRM1 cargo (see Figure 4), as is eRF1 (Supplementary file 2 and Bohnsack et al., 2002).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 and supported by citation.

claim: eRF1 is a CRM1 cargo.
source: The translation termination factor eRF3a is again a bona fide CRM1 cargo (see Figure 4), as is eRF1 (Supplementary file 2 and Bohnsack et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bohnsack et al., 2002.

claim: SRP54 appears to be the NES-carrying component of the signal recognition particle SRP.
source: Furthermore, CRM1-dependent nuclear depletion also applies to several translation-associated factors, such as the signal recognition particle SRP, where SRP54 appears to be the NES-carrying component (Figure 7), or the human start-methionine aminopeptidase MetAP2, which binds translating ribosomes and cleaves the start methionine from nascent polypeptides.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7.

claim: MetAP2 accumulates upon leptomycin B treatment in nucleoli.
source: The normally strictly cytoplasmic MetAP2 accumulates upon leptomycin B treatment in nucleoli (Figure 7), not only validating it as a true CRM1 cargo, but also suggesting that it can bind to assembling ribosomal subunits prematurely and possibly interfere with the maturation process.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7.

claim: MetAP2 can bind to assembling ribosomal subunits prematurely and possibly interfere with the maturation process.
source: The normally strictly cytoplasmic MetAP2 accumulates upon leptomycin B treatment in nucleoli (Figure 7), not only validating it as a true CRM1 cargo, but also suggesting that it can bind to assembling ribosomal subunits prematurely and possibly interfere with the maturation process.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the nucleolar accumulation.

claim: CRM1 is essential for ribosome biogenesis.
source: CRM1 is known to be essential for ribosome biogenesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge.

claim: CRM1 exports pre-60S ribosomal subunits through the export adapter Nmd3.
source: It exports pre-60S ribosomal subunits (rSUs) through the export adapter Nmd3 (Ho et al., 2000), while Ltv1 and Rio2 behave like export adapters for yeast 40S rSUs (Seiser et al., 2006; Fischer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ho et al., 2000.

claim: Ltv1 and Rio2 behave like export adapters for yeast 40S rSUs.
source: It exports pre-60S ribosomal subunits (rSUs) through the export adapter Nmd3 (Ho et al., 2000), while Ltv1 and Rio2 behave like export adapters for yeast 40S rSUs (Seiser et al., 2006; Fischer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Seiser et al., 2006 and Fischer et al., 2015.

claim: Yeast Enp1 behaves like an autonomous CRM1 substrate.
source: We now found that yeast Enp1 (essential nuclear protein 1) behaves like an autonomous CRM1 substrate (Figure 8), suggesting that it might actually act as yet another adapter for CRM1-mediated export of 40S rSUs.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8.

claim: Enp1 might act as yet another adapter for CRM1-mediated export of 40S rSUs.
source: We now found that yeast Enp1 (essential nuclear protein 1) behaves like an autonomous CRM1 substrate (Figure 8), suggesting that it might actually act as yet another adapter for CRM1-mediated export of 40S rSUs.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Additional predominantly nuclear ribosomal biogenesis factors behave like CRM1 cargoes, including Brx1, Pno1, Tsr1, Rpf1, Rlp7, Ytm1, Tsr3, Rix7, Erb1, Nsa1, Ssf1, Dim1, Nol10, Loc1, and Rpf2.
source: Furthermore, our analysis revealed that additional predominantly nuclear, ribosomal biogenesis factors behave like CRM1 cargoes, namely: Brx1, Pno1, Tsr1, Rpf1, Rlp7, Ytm1, Tsr3, Rix7, Erb1, Nsa1, Ssf1, Dim1, Nol10, Loc1, and Rpf2 (see Supplementary file 4 sheet 'Ribosome biogenesis').
evidence: This is based on the CRM1 binding data.

claim: Drg1, Rei1, Reh1, Lsg1, and Ria1 showed a strong and strictly RanGTP-dependent interaction with CRM1.
source: All these factors showed a strong and strictly RanGTP-dependent interaction with CRM1 (Supplementary file 4 sheet 'Ribosome biogenesis').
evidence: This is based on the CRM1 binding data.

claim: CRM1 keeps cytoplasmic ribosomal maturation factors cytoplasmic, possibly to avoid the occurrence of translation-active ribosomes inside the nucleus.
source: This suggests that CRM1 keeps them cytoplasmic, possibly to avoid the occurrence of translation-active ribosomes inside the nucleus (at least Lsg1 and Rei1 behave like true CRM1 cargoes, see Figure 8).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Lsg1 and Rei1 behave like true CRM1 cargoes.
source: This suggests that CRM1 keeps them cytoplasmic, possibly to avoid the occurrence of translation-active ribosomes inside the nucleus (at least Lsg1 and Rei1 behave like true CRM1 cargoes, see Figure 8).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8.

claim: Cytoplasmic maturation factors displace the export mediators Arx1, Nmd3, Mex67, and Mtr2 from newly exported 60S species.
source: A cytoplasmic confinement of these factors appears crucial for yet another reason: They displace the export mediators Arx1, Nmd3, Mex67, and Mtr2 from newly exported 60S species (Loibl et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Loibl et al., 2014.

claim: A premature intra-nuclear displacement by mis-localized cytoplasmic maturation factors could abort ribosomal export.
source: A premature intra-nuclear displacement by mis-localized cytoplasmic maturation factors could thus abort ribosomal export.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the function of these factors.

claim: rpS3 is highly abundant in the 'CRM1+RanGTP'-bound fraction.
source: Cytoplasmic maturation also involves the incorporation of additional ribosomal proteins, a prominent example being rpS3. rpS3 is highly abundant in the 'CRM1+RanGTP'-bound fraction, and thus perhaps hindered (directly or indirectly) by CRM1 to bind 40S rSUs prematurely already inside nuclei.
evidence: This is based on the CRM1 binding data.

claim: rpS3 is perhaps hindered by CRM1 to bind 40S rSUs prematurely already inside nuclei.
source: rpS3 is highly abundant in the 'CRM1+RanGTP'-bound fraction, and thus perhaps hindered (directly or indirectly) by CRM1 to bind 40S rSUs prematurely already inside nuclei.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Aminoacyl tRNA ligases show a strong cytoplasmic bias in Xenopus oocytes.
source: To clarify this issue at least for Xenopus oocytes, we analysed the nucleocytoplasmic distribution of the aminoacyl tRNA ligases and found a strong cytoplasmic bias (Figure 9C; Supplementary file 2, sheet 'Aminoacyl tRNA ligases').
evidence: This is based on the nucleocytoplasmic partitioning data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The cytoplasmic concentration of aminoacyl tRNA ligases exceeded the nuclear one by more than a factor of 100 in most cases.
source: The cytoplasmic concentration exceeded the nuclear one by more than a factor of 100 in most cases, and even the least excluded ones had ≈10 times higher levels in the cytoplasm than in the nucleus.
evidence: This is based on the nucleocytoplasmic partitioning data.

claim: It is rather unlikely that nuclear aminoacylation is a general proof-reading criterion prior to tRNA export.
source: This makes is rather unlikely that nuclear aminoacylation is a general proof-reading criterion prior to tRNA export.
evidence: This is inferred from the strong cytoplasmic bias of aminoacyl tRNA ligases.

claim: The Ser, Thre, and Asn tRNA-ligases showed a strong RanGTP-dependent interaction with CRM1.
source: At least the Ser, Thre, and Asn tRNA-ligases showed a strong RanGTP-dependent interaction with CRM1.
evidence: This is based on the CRM1 binding data.

claim: Xenopus Asn tRNA ligase shows a perfect CRM1-dependent nuclear exclusion.
source: We tested the Xenopus Asn tRNA ligase by transfection assays and observed a perfect CRM1-dependent nuclear exclusion (Figure 6).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6.

claim: Human Ser tRNA ligase shows a CRM1-dependent nuclear exclusion.
source: Human Ser tRNA ligase and the α-subunit of the yeast Phe tRNA ligase behave the same way (Figures 7 and 8), suggesting that cells make a true effort to keep tRNA aminoacylation cytoplasmic.
evidence: This is shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: The α-subunit of the yeast Phe tRNA ligase shows a CRM1-dependent nuclear exclusion.
source: Human Ser tRNA ligase and the α-subunit of the yeast Phe tRNA ligase behave the same way (Figures 7 and 8), suggesting that cells make a true effort to keep tRNA aminoacylation cytoplasmic.
evidence: This is shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Cells make a true effort to keep tRNA aminoacylation cytoplasmic.
source: Human Ser tRNA ligase and the α-subunit of the yeast Phe tRNA ligase behave the same way (Figures 7 and 8), suggesting that cells make a true effort to keep tRNA aminoacylation cytoplasmic.
evidence: This is inferred from the CRM1-dependent nuclear exclusion of multiple tRNA ligases.

claim: Human Cys tRNA ligase failed to interact with CRM1.
source: We also tested the human Cys tRNA ligase that failed to interact with CRM1 (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on the CRM1 binding data.

claim: The transfected GFP-fusion of human Cys tRNA ligase showed a perfect nuclear exclusion, which was also not impaired by leptomycin B-treatment.
source: Nevertheless, the transfected GFP-fusion protein showed a perfect nuclear exclusion, which was also not impaired by leptomycin B-treatment (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Several high-scoring CRM1 cargoes were identified amongst cytoplasmic mRNA degradation factors, components of P-bodies and stress granules.
source: We identified several high-scoring CRM1 cargoes amongst cytoplasmic mRNA degradation factors, components of P-bodies and stress granules.
evidence: This is based on the CRM1 binding data.

claim: Upf1, Upf2 and Upf3 are high-scoring CRM1 cargoes.
source: These include Upf1, Upf2 and Upf3 (Supplementary files 2–4 and Figure 5), which function in nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) of incorrectly spliced mRNA during a pioneering round of translation (reviewed by Popp and Maquat, 2013), as well as the de-capping enzymes (DCP1 and DCP2) and enhancers of de-capping (EDC proteins), which typically reside within P-granules and initiate mRNA degradation (reviewed by Parker and Sheth, 2007).
evidence: This is based on the CRM1 binding data shown in Figure 5.

claim: CRM1 probably enables cells to control nuclear and cytoplasmic RNA turnover independently from each other.
source: Thus, CRM1 probably enables cells to control nuclear and cytoplasmic RNA turnover independently from each other.
evidence: This is inferred from the identification of mRNA degradation factors as CRM1 cargoes.

claim: COPI and COPII coat proteins behave like CRM1 cargoes.
source: Yet, we observed that COPI and COPII coat proteins as well as, e.g., the AP-1 and AP2 adapter complexes or the AP180 clathrin coat assembly protein behave like CRM1 cargoes (Supplementary files 2–3, sheets 'Vesicle coat proteins'; as well as Figures 4 and 6).
evidence: This is based on the CRM1 binding data.

claim: Vesicle coat proteins are extremely well excluded from the oocyte nucleus.
source: They are also extremely well excluded from the oocyte nucleus (Figure 9E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9E.

claim: The absence of intranuclear vesicles in most cell types can be explained by an active depletion of the vesicular budding machineries from the nuclear interior.
source: The absence in other cell types can now be explained by an active depletion of the vesicular budding machineries from the nuclear interior.
evidence: This is inferred from the identification of vesicle coat proteins as CRM1 cargoes.

claim: Atg1, Atg13, Atg17, and Vps30 are all required for autophagy in yeast and all of them are high-scoring CRM1 cargoes.
source: Atg1, Atg13, Atg17, and Vps30 are all required for autophagy in yeast and all of them are high-scoring CRM1 cargoes (Supplementary file 4, sheet 'Autophagy').
evidence: This is based on the CRM1 binding data.

claim: CRM1 appears to counteract an initiation of autophagy from the nuclear interior.
source: It thus appears as if CRM1 counteracted an initiation of autophagy from the nuclear interior.
evidence: This is inferred from the identification of autophagy factors as CRM1 cargoes.

claim: The ATG8-conjugating enzyme ATG3 is a major CRM1-cargo in human cells.
source: For example, here the ATG8-conjugating enzyme ATG3 is a major CRM1-cargo (Figure 7).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7.

claim: The peroxisomal targeting (PTS1) receptor Pex5 was identified as a high-scoring CRM1-binder.
source: The peroxisomal targeting (PTS1) receptor Pex5 was not only identified as a high-scoring CRM1-binder, but also showed a strictly CRM1-dependent nuclear exclusion (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on the CRM1 binding data and shown in Figure 7.

claim: Pex5 showed a strictly CRM1-dependent nuclear exclusion.
source: The peroxisomal targeting (PTS1) receptor Pex5 was not only identified as a high-scoring CRM1-binder, but also showed a strictly CRM1-dependent nuclear exclusion (Figure 7).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7.

claim: PEX19 from yeast or human behaves like a perfect CRM1 cargo and shows a CRM1-dependent nuclear exclusion.
source: PEX19 from yeast or human is another example, which behaves like a perfect CRM1 cargo and shows a CRM1-dependent nuclear exclusion (Figures 7 and 8).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: A mis-targeting of PEX19 to nuclei by a fused NLS causes nuclear accumulation of newly synthesised peroxisomal membrane proteins.
source: A mis-targeting of PEX19 to nuclei by a fused NLS causes interesting consequences, namely nuclear accumulation of newly synthesised peroxisomal membrane proteins (Sacksteder et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sacksteder et al., 2000.

claim: A loss of CRM1-mediated export would likely cause nuclear accumulation of newly synthesised peroxisomal membrane proteins.
source: It now seems very likely that a loss of CRM1-mediated export would have the same effect.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavior of PEX19 when mis-targeted to nuclei.

claim: Xenopus and human septins are highly abundant amongst the CRM1-bound proteins.
source: Xenopus and human septins, in contrast, are highly abundant amongst the CRM1-bound proteins.
evidence: This is based on the CRM1 binding data.

claim: Septin 2 was validated as a CRM1 cargo.
source: We validated Septin 2 and found that leptomycin B treatment of transfected cells caused indeed a shift from a cytoplasmic to a nuclear localisation (Figure 5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5.

claim: High-scoring CRM1 cargoes were found amongst the components of the centrosomes.
source: We further found high-scoring CRM1 cargoes amongst the components of the centrosomes (Figure 9F), which function as microtubule organizing centres (reviewed by Bornens, 2012).
evidence: This is based on the CRM1 binding data shown in Figure 9F.

claim: Strong CRM1 interactors include the HAUS augmin complex, γ-tubulin and γ-tubulin complex components as well as a number of additional centriolar proteins.
source: These strong CRM1 interactors include the HAUS augmin complex, γ-tubulin and γ-tubulin complex components as well as a number of additional centriolar proteins (e.g. CEP41, CEP55, and CEP170).
evidence: This is based on the CRM1 binding data.

claim: CRM1 might actively suppress microtubule nucleation in metazoan interphase nuclei.
source: This could point not only to an active suppression of microtubule nucleation in metazoan interphase nuclei, but also to additional mitotic function of CRM1 (see Arnaoutov et al., 2005)—namely at centrosomes.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Approximately 70 kinases were found as high-scoring CRM1 cargoes in HeLa cells.
source: Alone in HeLa cells, we found ≈ 70 kinases as high-scoring CRM1 cargoes (Supplementary file 3), only a fraction of which had been described as such before.
evidence: This is based on the CRM1 binding data.

claim: New CRM1 cargo kinases include protein kinase A, the interleukin-1 receptor-associated kinase 1, the pro-apoptotic serine/ threonine kinase 3, the tank-binding kinase 1, Raf-1, and several isoforms of casein kinase I and II.
source: The new cargoes include heavily studied kinases such as protein kinase A, the interleukin-1 receptor-associated kinase 1, the pro-apoptotic serine/ threonine kinase 3, the tank-binding kinase 1, Raf-1, and several isoforms of casein kinase I and II.
evidence: This is based on the CRM1 binding data.

claim: Numerous kinase regulators were identified as new CRM1 cargoes, including the regulatory subunit of PKA (PRKAr2a) and the TSC1•TSC2 complex.
source: In addition, we identified numerous kinase regulators as new CRM1 cargoes, examples being the already mentioned regulatory subunit of PKA (PRKAr2a; Figures 4 and 5) or the TSC1•TSC2 complex (Supplementary file 2), which is a key component of the mTOR signalling pathway (Laplante and Sabatini, 2009).
evidence: This is based on the CRM1 binding data.

claim: CRM1 action will contribute to compartment-specific phosphorylation patterns.
source: Such action of CRM1 will contribute to compartment-specific phosphorylation patterns, but in many cases also exert control by granting or denying those kinases access to their substrates.
evidence: This is inferred from the identification of kinases and kinase regulators as CRM1 cargoes.

claim: 22 phosphatases were identified as potential new CRM1 cargoes in human cells.
source: Likewise, numerous phosphatases and components of the ubiquitin or the ubiquitin-like modifier system showed up as potential new CRM1 cargoes, alone in human cells 22 and 57, respectively (Supplementary file 3, Figure 9H and 9K).
evidence: This is based on the CRM1 binding data.

claim: 57 components of the ubiquitin or the ubiquitin-like modifier system were identified as potential new CRM1 cargoes in human cells.
source: Likewise, numerous phosphatases and components of the ubiquitin or the ubiquitin-like modifier system showed up as potential new CRM1 cargoes, alone in human cells 22 and 57, respectively (Supplementary file 3, Figure 9H and 9K).
evidence: This is based on the CRM1 binding data.

claim: The most common NES pattern is a PKI-type NES.
source: The most common one is a PKI-type NES.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NES patterns.

claim: NESs were successfully identified in six validated CRM1 cargoes.
source: We applied these criteria to identify NESs in a set of validated, new CRM1 cargoes. We were successful in six cases (Figure 5), but failed with some others (e.g. Pex5, rpS3, Haus1, Cop beta', MetAP2, CDC37L, Enp1, Phe tRNA ligase α).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5.

claim: NES identification failed for some validated CRM1 cargoes including Pex5, rpS3, Haus1, Cop beta', MetAP2, CDC37L, Enp1, and Phe tRNA ligase α.
source: We applied these criteria to identify NESs in a set of validated, new CRM1 cargoes. We were successful in six cases (Figure 5), but failed with some others (e.g. Pex5, rpS3, Haus1, Cop beta', MetAP2, CDC37L, Enp1, Phe tRNA ligase α).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the NES prediction approach.

claim: The study provides a total of approximately 1300 'category A cargoes', which should contain an NES.
source: First, we provide large test sets for benchmarking current and future NES predictions, first of all a total of ≈1300 'category A cargoes', which should contain an NES (in the case of oligomers at least one per complex).
evidence: This is based on the classification of CRM1 cargoes.

claim: The study found approximately 2200 clear non-CRM1-binders that can serve as a negative control group for NES prediction.
source: We also found ≈2200 clear non-CRM1-binders that can serve as a negative control group for NES prediction.
evidence: This is based on the classification of proteins that did not bind CRM1.

claim: Seven conflicting cases between this study and NESdb were re-tested and all behaved as predicted from their classification as CRM1 non-binders.
source: To address this issue, we analysed seven of these conflicting cases and tested the behaviour of the corresponding GFP fusions in the HeLa cell transfection assay (Figure 7—figure supplement 1). All of them showed a considerable nuclear signal already in untreated cells and this nuclear signal did not further increase upon blocking CRM1 by leptomycin B.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cyclin B is kept cytoplasmic by CRM1 until prophase, when the NES gets inactivated by phosphorylation of adjacent serine residues.
source: Cyclin B, for example, is kept cytoplasmic by CRM1 until prophase, when the NES gets inactivated by phosphorylation of adjacent serine residues and the protein suddenly accumulates inside nuclei (Yang et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yang et al., 1998.

claim: PHAX requires phosphorylation for an efficient interaction with CRM1.
source: PHAX, the export adapter for U snRNAs, on the other hand, requires phosphorylation for an efficient interaction with CRM1 (Kitao et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kitao et al., 2008.

claim: The majority of CRM1 cargoes are actually exclusively cytoplasmic proteins.
source: Surprising outcomes of our study not only were the sheer number of CRM1 cargoes (≈ 1/4 of all detectable cytoplasmic and nuclear proteins), but also that the majority of cargoes are actually exclusively cytoplasmic proteins (Figure 9A; Supplementary files 2–4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9A and the supplementary files.

claim: CRM1 cargoes represent approximately 1/4 of all detectable cytoplasmic and nuclear proteins.
source: Surprising outcomes of our study not only were the sheer number of CRM1 cargoes (≈ 1/4 of all detectable cytoplasmic and nuclear proteins), but also that the majority of cargoes are actually exclusively cytoplasmic proteins (Figure 9A; Supplementary files 2–4).
evidence: This is calculated from the total number of identified proteins and CRM1 cargoes.

claim: It is impossible to preclude nuclear entry of unwanted proteins in the first place because there are several leakage routes into the nucleus.
source: The perhaps best answer is that is impossible to preclude nuclear entry of unwanted proteins in the first place, because there are several leakage routes into the nucleus.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the properties of the NPC barrier.

claim: The NPC permeability barrier is based on the sieving effect of reversibly crosslinked FG repeat domains.
source: It is based on the sieving effect of reversibly crosslinked FG repeat domains and probably represents compromise in the sense that a tighter barrier would also restrict facilitated transport (see Schmidt and Görlich, 2015 and discussions therein).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schmidt and Görlich, 2015.

claim: The open mitosis in metazoans leads to a complete mixing of nuclear and cytoplasmic contents and requires an unmixing following reformation of the nuclear envelope.
source: The open mitosis in metazoans, for example, leads to a complete mixing of nuclear and cytoplasmic contents and requires an unmixing following reformation of the nuclear envelope.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitosis.

claim: Obligatory cytoplasmic proteins are subject to active nuclear export following open mitosis.
source: Nuclear proteins require re-import, while obligatory cytoplasmic proteins, such as translation factors, components of the vesicular transport machinery and many others, are obviously subject to active nuclear export.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the need to unmix nuclear and cytoplasmic contents after mitosis.

claim: Nuclear envelope damage occurs rather frequently in certain cultured cancer cells.
source: Finally, cells should survive a temporary damage of their nuclear envelope, which is known to occur rather frequently in certain cultured cancers cells (Hatch et al., 2013), but might also happen in normal cells, in particular when exposed to mechanical stress.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hatch et al., 2013.

claim: The barriers of the NE alone cannot maintain the compartment identities.
source: Thus, the barriers of the NE alone cannot maintain the compartment identities.
evidence: This is inferred from the existence of multiple leakage routes into the nucleus.

claim: A robust separation of nuclear and cytoplasmic contents requires active corrective mechanisms, whereby the exportin CRM1 appears to play a very central role.
source: Instead, a robust separation of nuclear and cytoplasmic contents requires active corrective mechanisms, whereby the exportin CRM1 appears to play a very central role.
evidence: This is inferred from the large number of CRM1 cargoes identified in the study.

claim: Xenopus laevis stage VI oocytes were dissected into nuclear and cytoplasmic fractions.
source: Manual microdissection of the oocytes was performed in '5:1/HEPES buffer' (10 mM HEPES/ KOH pH 7.5, 83 mM KCl, 17 mM NaCl, supplemented with Roche complete protease inhibitor (EDTA-free) as previously described (Liu and Liu, 2006).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used.

claim: Quantitative mass spectrometric analysis of the obtained nuclear and cytosolic fractions involved three biological replicates with two technical replicates each.
source: Quantitative mass spectrometric analysis of the obtained nuclear and cytosolic fractions involved three biological replicates with two technical replicates each.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: For quantification of nucleocytoplasmic partitioning, approximately 60 nuclei were compared with approximately 6 cytoplasms.
source: For quantification of nucleocytoplasmic partitioning, we considered that a nucleus is 10-fold smaller in volume than a yolk-free cytoplasm. Therefore, we compared for each analysis ≈60 nuclei with ≈6 cytoplasms.
evidence: This describes the experimental design accounting for volume differences.

claim: Universal Proteomics Standard-2 (UPS2) was added to the analysed samples at a 1:10 (w/w) ratio between the standards and the total sample protein.
source: To estimate absolute protein concentrations, Universal Proteomics Standard-2 (UPS2; Sigma-Aldrich) was added to the analysed samples (at a 1:10 (w/w) ratio between the standards and the total sample protein).
evidence: This describes the method for absolute protein quantification.

claim: The mass spectrometry proteomics data have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE partner repository with the dataset identifier PXD002899.
source: The mass spectrometry proteomics data have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium (Vizcaíno et al., 2014) via the PRIDE partner repository with the dataset identifier PXD002899.
evidence: This describes where the data are deposited.

claim: The dataset of high confidence CRM1 interactions has been submitted to the IntAct databases with the identifier IM-24624.
source: The dataset of high confidence CRM1 interactions (cargo categories A, B, and 'low abundance') has been submitted to the IntAct databases (Orchard et al., 2014) with the identifier IM-24624.
evidence: This describes where the interaction data are deposited.
